15

Hiring & People Systems

Applicant tracking setup, onboarding workflow automation, role scorecards, and performance-tracking infrastructure: the systems layer of an HR function without the HR-consulting overhead.

How it works

Assess, train in context, sustain.

Enablement runs in three stages. We start with where the team actually is, not where the deployment plan assumed they'd be, and build from there.

Step 1

Assess Fluency

Where the team is, role by role. Not a survey. A structured read of current behavior, resistance, and the specific gaps each role will face when the systems go live.

Step 2

Train in Context

On the actual systems we built, in the actual workflows your team runs. Not generic AI literacy. Specific fluency for the tools and agents in their daily work.

Step 3

Sustain

Policy, coaching, and the systemic supervisor model so adoption holds beyond launch. The org becomes self-reinforcing rather than dependent on ongoing training events.

In practice

We built the firm this way. The team is the proof.

RAND's root-cause research on failed AI projects found the dominant failure modes were organizational, not technical: leadership misunderstanding the problem, weak data foundations, and teams that never adopted the tools. The model worked. The org didn't adapt. That finding is the foundation of this practice.

Zanwik operates AI-native already. The founding team runs this model internally. Technical execution is led by a May 2026 graduate who grew up on these tools and built fluency alongside the architecture. The systemic supervisor model isn't a training curriculum we wrote for clients. It's how we run.

## Software Consolidation & SaaS Cost Cutting | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/services/consolidation

Services / Systems Consolidation
Services · Systems Consolidation

Sometimes the fix isn't another tool. It's killing five of them.

The average company runs 130 SaaS apps and uses a fraction of what it pays for. We audit the sprawl, then replace, eliminate, and consolidate, building custom only where off-the-shelf genuinely fails. Less surface area, lower cost, one architecture. Whether you run a dozen tools or a hundred, if some overlap and some quietly cost you, this is where we look.

Book a diagnostic → All services

What's included

The consolidation work, named.

Every component from the audit through the cutover. Consolidation doesn't end when the tools are chosen. It ends when the data is clean, the subscriptions are cancelled, and the team is running one architecture.

01

Tool & SaaS Audit

Every tool you run, every seat you pay for, and every overlap mapped in one inventory. Most organizations don't know what they're running until they see it all in one place.

02

Software Rationalization

The keep / replace / eliminate decision for every tool, with the cost math, the capability gap analysis, and a clear recommendation for each. Not a suggestion list. A decision map.

03

Consolidation onto One Architecture

Replace the survivors' siloed data with a unified data model. One source of truth, one integration surface, one architecture everything plugs into going forward.

04

Custom Builds Where Off-the-Shelf Can't Fit

Some gaps genuinely require a custom build. We build only where nothing off-the-shelf fits, and we're honest when something off-the-shelf is the right answer.

05

Data Migration & Integrity

Everything in the tools you're killing gets moved cleanly. Data integrity is non-negotiable: migration is part of the engagement, not an afterthought.

06

Contract & Cost Takeout

Kill the subscriptions you don't need. We identify contracts with near-term renewal dates, negotiate exits where possible, and remove recurring cost that isn't earning its keep.

07

Integration of Survivors into One Source of Truth

The tools you keep get connected: bi-directional sync, unified data model, no more copy-paste between systems.

08

Change Management for the Cutover

The humans running the old tools need to know how the new ones work. We manage the transition so nothing breaks and no one is left on a tool that's been turned off.

09

License & Seat Audit

Every paid seat across every tool accounted for: who's active, who hasn't logged in for 90 days, and which seats are provisioned to roles that no longer exist.

10

Redundancy Mapping

Capabilities that exist in two or more tools identified and mapped, so the keep/replace decision is made with a complete picture of what each tool actually does for which team.

11

Single-Sign-On Consolidation

Authentication rationalized to a single identity provider, so access provisioning and de-provisioning happen once, in one place, with a complete audit trail.

12

Integration Rationalization

Every point-to-point integration between tools inventoried, and the integration architecture redesigned around the consolidated stack, so retired tools don't leave broken connections behind.

13

Vendor-Contract Renegotiation

Near-term renewals identified and negotiated from an informed position, with actual usage data, the consolidated tool map, and a clear picture of what leverage exists at renewal time.

14

Decommissioning & Change Management

A structured shutdown sequence for each retired tool: data extracted, users migrated, contracts terminated, and the organization moved to the replacement without productivity loss.

15

Post-Acquisition Integration

When two companies combine, the first six months are a systems war. We run the integration playbook: consolidate the CRMs, unify reporting, migrate data, kill duplicate software, and build the combined operating layer.

How it works

Inventory, rationalize, consolidate.

Three stages. Each one is a decision gate: you see the full picture before any tool is killed or any build is started. No surprises, no forced migrations.

Step 1

Inventory

Every tool, every seat, every dollar. Most organizations haven't seen their full stack in one view. This is the map. It's the deliverable that makes the rationalization possible.

Step 2

Rationalize

The keep / replace / eliminate decision for every tool, with the cost math. We run the analysis; you make the call. Nothing is deprecated without a clear recommendation and your sign-off.

Step 3

Consolidate

Migrate the data, integrate the survivors, shut the rest off cleanly. Change management included: the team runs the new architecture from day one.

In practice

A 1.5% fee replaced by a custom flow and a lower-cost processor.

Context-switching across 130 apps costs the US economy an estimated $450 billion per year. The average knowledge worker loses roughly 200 hours annually just switching between tools, time that compounds into missed deadlines, duplicated data, and work that falls through the gaps between systems.

What this looks like in practice: a client-management tool charging a 1.5% transaction fee gets replaced with a low-cost ACH processor and a custom client-management flow built for the actual process, not a generic one. The fee disappears. The workflow gets tighter. The surface area shrinks. It is how you get to the $200/month stack that replaces the sprawl .

Questions

Straight answers.

Will you just tell us to buy more software?

The opposite. Our bias is to eliminate and consolidate. Every tool we recommend keeping has to justify itself against the custom alternative or the cheaper replacement. We build custom only where nothing off-the-shelf fits, and we say so plainly when off-the-shelf is the better answer.

What about the data in the tools we kill?

Migration and integrity are part of every consolidation engagement. Nothing is lost. Every record in every deprecated tool is either migrated to the surviving architecture or archived with a clear retrieval path.

How is this different from Token Governance?

Token Governance cuts AI spend: the cost of the models and workflows running in your stack. Consolidation cuts tool sprawl: the SaaS subscriptions, the duplicate capabilities, and the integration complexity. Together they strip cost and complexity out of the whole stack.

Services · On-Prem & Intelligence Sovereignty

What this means for your business

Your AI runs on a box in your building ,  not in a data center somewhere. You stop paying per-query cloud fees. Your sensitive documents, financial records, and internal processes never leave your property. The AI gets smarter every month as we update it. You own the hardware outright.

What it is

A physical AI system on your premises. Full stop.

This is not hosting. It is not hardware resale. It is Zanwik's architecture and intelligence layer running on hardware the client owns, on the client's property, with no data ever leaving the building.

The monthly cloud API bill goes to zero. The compliance exposure goes to zero. The AI gets better every month as open-weight models improve, on the same hardware, no migration.

01

Local inference layer

07

Air-gapped deployments

Full operation with no internet dependency. Model inference, retrieval, and workflows run entirely on-site, with no outbound API calls and no data leaving the building.

08

Local RAG over private data

Your documents, contracts, SOPs, and financial records indexed and queryable entirely on-premises. No data leaves the hardware, and the model knows your operation without cloud exposure.

Sensitive queries stay on-premises; non-sensitive queries route to cloud models where latency or capability matters, with a routing layer that enforces the policy automatically and logs every decision.

Security Hardening & Risk Baseline

Close the obvious gaps: access controls, secrets management, single sign-on, backup and disaster recovery, and document a security posture that survives an enterprise customer's vendor review.

The CFO argument

The math works faster than most CFOs expect.

At 10,000 queries per day and 500 tokens per query, a reasonable volume for a 20-person team, cloud API costs run between $450 and $2,250 per month depending on the model. On-prem inference runs about $50 per month in electricity.

The DGX Spark hardware at ~$4,699 pays for itself in 3 to 12 months depending on current cloud spend. After that, every query is free, forever, regardless of how much the model improves.

There is no migration cost when better open-weight models ship. We point the system at the new model and the upgrade is live. You don't pay for the improvement; you just benefit from it.

The ownership model

You own your intelligence. You don't rent it.

Zanwik charges for architecture, build, and maintenance. The hardware is yours. The data is yours. The AI is yours. The only thing that keeps you paying us is that we keep making it better, which is the incentive we want. The same lean-stack thinking drives the $200/month stack that replaces the sprawl .

Architecture and build

We design the intelligence layer, deploy the models, wire the retrieval and agent systems, and get everything running. That's the engagement.

Maintenance and evolution

Models improve constantly. We handle the upgrades, monitor performance, and evolve the system as the technology moves. You don't manage any of it.

No lock-in

You own every component. If you want to bring it in-house, the system is yours to hand off. We don't hold anything hostage.

In practice

Four industries where cloud AI is a liability.

These are typical scenarios in verticals where compliance, competitive exposure, or data-residency law makes cloud AI the wrong answer.

Golf resort operator

A resort operator builds their full financial model and pricing logic inside a cloud-hosted chatbot. A competitor with cloud access to the same API can extract the methodology. The on-prem answer: financial AI, concierge, and predictive ordering all running locally, cloud dependency gone.

40-attorney law firm

Attorney-client privilege makes cloud AI a liability, not an asset. A private legal-research layer with case-law retrieval and a full audit log of every query means associates get the answers while the firm keeps the privilege.

Multi-branch credit union

Examiners want a complete audit trail of AI-assisted decisions. An on-prem deployment with tamper-evident logs closes that conversation. Compliance posture improves; cloud AI spend goes to zero.

Questions

Straight answers.

Isn't on-prem AI worse than the big cloud models?

Open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen) are now strong enough for most business tasks: document Q&A, retrieval, summarization, classification, drafting. And we upgrade them free as better ones ship. The gap to frontier cloud models is narrowing every quarter, on the same hardware you already bought.

Do we have to buy the hardware?

Yes, and that's the point. You purchase it directly from the vendor; we never mark up hardware. You own the asset outright from day one. Our fee is architecture, build, and ongoing maintenance. There's no monthly lease, no subscription, no rent.

What if compliance is the blocker?

That's exactly the use case. Data never leaves your premises, query logs are yours, and the architecture is designed from the start around your data-residency and compliance requirements, not bolted on after.

## AI Cost Control & Spend Governance | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/services/token-governance

Services / Token Governance
Services · Token Governance

Do you know what your team's AI is costing you: per person, per month?

Almost nobody can answer that. Employees are querying AI tools all day with no visibility, no limits, no caching. They pay for the same question dozens of times. We put a meter on it, find the waste, and take a cut of what we save you. Zero risk on your end.

Book a diagnostic → All services

What it is

A governance layer between your employees and their AI tools.

Every query is logged, rate-limited, cached, and routed to the cheapest model capable of answering it. You get full visibility and control. You stop paying for the same question 40 times a day.

This is not a technology product. It is a cost-containment engagement. The CFO is the buyer. The trigger is the moment someone gave your team access to an AI tool with no follow-up about budgets or oversight. It pairs naturally with the $200/month stack that replaces the sprawl .

01

Full spend visibility

Every query attributed to a user and department. You see who is spending what, on which tools, and why.

02

Semantic caching

Queries similar to ones already answered return from cache in milliseconds at zero cost. The most common queries (often 30 to 50% of total volume) stop hitting the API.

03

Smart model routing

Simple questions go to cheap models. Complex ones go to expensive ones. The routing logic is tuned to your actual query patterns.

04

Rate limiting and budgets

Per-user and per-department monthly caps. No surprise bills. No individual running up the tab.

05

Compliance filters

Sensitive-data and PII detection, and custom content filters at the edge, before any query reaches an external model. When contracts limit where client data can go, this is the compliance product.

06

Monthly savings report

What the layer saved last month, in dollars. Your cut. Our cut. The running total since the engagement started.

07

Per-Team Budgets & Quotas

Monthly caps set by department, team, or individual, enforced at the proxy layer before the overage happens, not discovered in the billing statement after.

08

Model-Routing Policy

Explicit rules for which query types go to which models, tuned to your actual query mix so capability and cost are both optimized, not just one or the other.

09

Prompt-Caching Strategy

Identify the high-frequency, low-variance queries that are candidates for semantic caching, build the cache layer, and measure the hit rate. The fastest path to cost reduction in most deployments.

10

Usage Analytics & Chargeback

Per-department spend attribution with enough granularity to support internal chargeback or billable-matter allocation: the audit trail that makes AI spend a managed line item.

11

Shadow-AI Discovery

Surface the AI tools employees are using outside the governance layer: unauthorized subscriptions, personal API keys, browser extensions, so the spend picture is complete, not just the tools IT approved.

12

Vendor-Contract Rightsizing

Audit active AI vendor contracts against actual usage patterns and model capabilities, then right-size seats, tiers, and commitments at renewal, cutting spend without cutting capability.

How it works

Audit first. Govern second. Compound from there.

The audit produces the discovery report. The governance layer installs the savings. Ongoing management keeps them compounding. No commitment required until you see the audit.

01

30-day audit: the discovery report

We instrument your AI traffic for 30 days. The report names spend by user and department, identifies the queries running 40 times a day, surfaces questions going to expensive models that a cheaper one handles just as well, and calculates the cache-hit rate. You see exactly where the money is going before you commit to anything.

02

Governance layer deployment

We place a governance proxy between your employees and their AI tools. Every query is logged, rate-limited, cached, and routed to the cheapest model capable of answering it. The layer is invisible to users. In some cases it is faster, because repeated queries hit the cache instead of the API.

03

Ongoing governance: compounding savings

Usage patterns shift, models improve, new tools get added. The governance layer evolves with them. We monitor, tune routing rules, refresh cache logic, and report monthly on what it saved. The savings compound as the layer gets smarter about your operation.

Performance pricing

We only make real money when we save you real money.

Setup is a flat project fee covering the 30-day audit and governance layer deployment. After that, ongoing governance is priced as a percentage of monthly savings. The exact structure is scoped with you and put in writing before you commit.

The math is straightforward: semantic caching eliminates a significant share of redundant queries, smart routing moves cheap work to cheap models, and our cut is a fraction of what we save you. If the savings are real, the fee is real. If the meter finds nothing, you have lost almost nothing.

Example above is illustrative. Actual savings depend on query volume, model mix, cache-hit rate, and routing efficiency.

How it works

One build fee. One recurring fee. One compounding system.

The model is designed to be simple to understand and aligned to the value the architecture actually delivers. The bill grows when the revenue systems grow. The seat is justified by the dollar value it drives every month, not by the number of deliverables produced.

Layer 1

Build fee: one time per phase

Each agent running a revenue system adds to the monthly retainer. The bill is a direct proxy for the value running: if an agent stops driving value, it comes offline and the fee drops.

In practice

A retainer that grows as the agents come online, one revenue system at a time.

A building-products manufacturer signed a Phase 1 build: the foundation layer: data model, CRM architecture, and the first automation workflow. At go-live, the retainer started at the base architect fee with zero agents running. No agents, no agent fees.

The roadmap sequences five agents across phases: dead-list reactivation runs first, then sample follow-up, then stalled-quote recovery, then booking qualification, then review management. Each agent comes online in a defined phase, adds its fee to the retainer, and runs a specific revenue system. By the time all five are live, the bill reflects five active revenue systems running simultaneously.

The context that accumulates over that build timeline: the edge cases, the customer patterns, the business logic encoded in the agents, the integration architecture, cannot be handed to a new firm and rebuilt in less than six to twelve months. That context is the structural moat. It is what the embedded model is designed to build.

Questions

Straight answers.

What's the difference between the embedded seat and a maintenance retainer?

A maintenance retainer keeps builds alive. An embedded seat runs revenue systems. The distinction is in what we're accountable for: a retainer is accountable for uptime; a seat is accountable for dollar outcomes. We report monthly on what the systems drove: revenue generated, costs eliminated, time recovered. If the report doesn't show value, the engagement gets restructured until it does. That accountability is what separates a seat from a retainer.

How does the engagement deepen over time?

The roadmap is designed in full at the strategy phase and executed phase by phase. By Phase 3, the architecture reflects 12 to 18 months of context about your operation, your edge cases, your customers, and your technology. A competitor starting fresh would take 6 to 12 months to rebuild that context, and they would rebuild it by making the mistakes we already made and corrected. Depth compounds. That is the structural moat.

What does 'biweekly cadence' mean operationally?

We are in your operating rhythm, not on-call for tickets. The biweekly call is structured: what the systems drove, what changed, what the next phase requires. Between calls we watch the architecture, not your inbox: observability dashboards, cost, drift. Day-to-day operation belongs to your team, and we make sure they can carry it.

Do you become our IT support team?

No, and that is deliberate. Every build ships with documentation, runbooks, and training so your team, or your in-house IT, knows exactly how to run it. Architecture stewardship is our job: what to upgrade, what to retire, what to build next. If you would rather not carry day-to-day operations at all, a structured managed-service plan is available as a separate, scoped engagement, with defined coverage and response terms instead of an open-ended help desk.

## Building-Materials Manufacturer: Case Study | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/work/building-materials-manufacturer

Work / Building-Materials Manufacturer
Case Study · Building materials manufacturing

Built on a single distributor. Then the distributor broke the commercial model.

A national-scale specialty manufacturer with a 15,000-contact list, no CRM, and zero conversion tracking. We're rebuilding the foundation, with a five-agent roadmap ready to deploy on top of it.

Book a diagnostic → See all work

The situation

A distribution monopoly, broken. Everything downstream of it, too.

The manufacturer had scaled to meaningful revenue through a single channel partner, a concentrated, efficient model that worked until it didn't. The partner began forcing markups that made the product uncompetitive at the end-customer level. The manufacturer brought distribution in-house and emerged on the other side needing to build direct-to-market capability from scratch.

The digital layer had never needed to work before. The distributor handled demand. Now it had to. What we found: two live domains on a legacy page-builder stack; no CRM; no conversion tracking; a 15,000-contact email list sitting dormant with no platform and no authentication. The company had a genuine price and performance advantage over the alternatives, and no mechanism to communicate it.

The single highest-ROI asset in the business was the dormant list. But before a single email could send, the foundation had to be sound: domains consolidated, data captured correctly, calculators live, tracking in place. You don't deploy agents on a broken foundation.

What we architected

Foundation first. Intelligence layer second. Agents third.

The engagement runs Foundation→Crawl→Walk. Each phase is independently scoped and independently deliverable. Phase 1 is the machine. The agents are the sales force. It brings together the connected systems foundation , the five-agent architecture , and back-office automation .

Foundation (Phase 1)

Full rebuild. Every system replaced or wired from scratch.

01

Platform migration

Legacy CMS and page-builder stack → modern web stack with a headless CMS. A 301 redirect map executed before DNS cutover so no existing link broke in the transition. Subdomain folded into the primary domain. Core Web Vitals rebuilt from scratch.

02

Conversion infrastructure

A materials-estimation calculator for project sizing and an instant-quote calculator feeding a lead form. A Command Center CRM-lite for inbound lead management. GA4, GTM, and a reporting dashboard wired for full conversion visibility. Baseline zero tracking became complete attribution.

03

List re-platforming

About 9,000 verified contacts migrated to a transactional email platform with full domain authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), segmentation by source and recency, and suppression lists built before a single send. The list is live and deployable.

04

Knowledge infrastructure

A single-tenant Knowledge Wiki, voice-matched to the owner, containing product specs, competitor comparisons, FAQ responses, and sales objection answers. Built as the knowledge base every downstream agent will query.

Intelligence Layer + Agents (Crawl → Walk)

Five-agent roadmap deploying onto the foundation Phase 1 built.

01

List reactivation agent

Reactivates the 15,000-contact list with sequenced outreach , with past customers, prospects, and cold contacts in separate tracks. Personalized at segment level, not blast level. Feeds qualified intent signals back to the CRM.

02

Social & content agent

Generates and schedules product content, comparison posts, and educational material pulling from the Knowledge Wiki. Maintains publishing cadence without human authorship per post.

03

Lead qualification agent

24/7 inbound qualifier. Handles inquiry volume, asks structured questions, routes hot leads to the owner, and captures cold leads into nurture sequences, without a human in the loop at 11pm.

04

Back-office & ops agent

Reconciles order data against current inventory positions, flags margin anomalies, and generates weekly operating summaries. The owner sees the business clearly without assembling a spreadsheet.

05

Dedicated secondary-product-line agent

Focused entirely on a secondary revenue stream that had been generating six figures with zero marketing effort. Handles inquiry, qualification, and proposal sequencing for the highest-margin product line in the catalog.

Outcomes

Real figures from the engagement. Projections labeled.

Phase 1 is in active build. Baseline metrics are real. Pipeline projections carry the Illustrative label.

~9,000

Verified contacts migrated, authenticated, and segmented, from a list the client estimated at 15,000. Ready to deploy.

## Custom Cabin Builder: Case Study | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/work/custom-cabin-builder

Work / Custom Cabin Builder
Case Study · Residential construction / tiny homes

Configure. Price. Propose. Sign. Deposit. Phase 1 live. Phase 2 designed.

A specialty cabin manufacturer selling configured structures across a full lineup of models, by phone and in-person, with manual re-entry at every step. Phase 1, a live-priced configurator for the full lineup, has run since April 2026. Phase 2 automates the path from proposal to signed contract to ACH deposit.

Book a diagnostic → See all work

The situation

A full model lineup. Manual proposals. A disconnected handoff at every step.

The manufacturer sells custom-configured cabins across a wide price range, from entry-level to premium, through direct sales and a multi-dealer channel. Deals happened on the phone and in person. After a customer configured their structure, the proposal process ran through their general-purpose client-management tool at 1.5% per transaction, disconnected from whatever the customer had configured. A salesperson would take the verbal spec, rebuild it in that tool, export a PDF, email it, follow up for a signature, and then handle the deposit separately. Every step was manual re-entry.

Field salespeople had no mobile proposal tool and no way to close at a customer's property without going back to a desk. Content and model pricing edits required a developer, so marketing was bottlenecked on engineering availability. The gap between "customer shows interest" and "deposit collected" was measured in days and depended entirely on who followed up.

The pattern to fix it was Data Change → Generate Document → Collect Signature + Payment. The question was how many handoffs could be eliminated inside a single session. The answer turned out to be all of them.

What we architected

Foundation: the configurator. Autonomous workflow: the pipeline.

Two phases. Phase 1 is the configurator itself, the foundation the entire sales process sits on. Phase 2 is Proposal Mode: the automated pipeline from draft to signature to deposit that runs without a human after the salesperson hits submit. It spans the product configurator , the automated proposal pipeline , and custom product engineering .

Phase 1: Configurator Foundation

The full model lineup, live pricing, dealer mode, and no-code admin control.

01

Model configurator

Exterior visualization with live pricing across the full cabin lineup. Customers select model, size, options, and add-ons. The price updates in real time. No phone call required to get a number.

02

Dealer mode

A dealer-specific view with separate pricing logic, so the direct-to-consumer and dealer channels run off the same configurator without polluting each other's pricing.

03

Admin panel for no-code pricing

Marketing can update model pricing, option costs, and availability from an admin panel with no developer required. The bottleneck on content and pricing changes is eliminated.

04

ACH deposit (designed, not yet live)

A deposit via ACH payments at 0.8% capped at $5, replacing the client-management tool's 1.5% with no cap. Designed to collect at configuration time, before a proposal is even generated. Planned infrastructure cost: ~$20/mo.

Phase 2: Proposal Pipeline

Draft→review→submit→sign→deposit in one session. Mobile for field sales.

01

Proposal Mode

Salesperson looks up a customer, toggles a discount if applicable, and reviews the configuration. One button generates a branded HTML + PDF proposal and sends it via transactional email with no re-entry of spec, no copy-paste from a config into a template.

02

E-signature

Embedded e-signature at ~$5/mo, a fraction of the legacy document-generation platform cost. The proposal includes a signature block; signature triggers automatic ACH deposit. Customer signs; deposit collects. No follow-up required.

03

Proposals dashboard

Full lifecycle view: draft, sent, signed, deposited, lapsed. Every proposal's status in one screen. A managed data layer with operations-visibility sync for the team.

04

Mobile-responsive for field sales

The full Proposal Mode runs in a mobile browser. A field salesperson at a customer's property can configure, generate the proposal, get the signature, and collect the deposit without leaving the conversation.

05

Headless CMS for content ownership

Marketing edits model descriptions, copy, and images through a headless CMS with no code, no developer dependency, no two-day turnaround on a price update.

Outcomes

What's live, and what's modeled.

Phase 1, the configurator, is live. Phase 2 is designed but not yet built, so its payment savings and costs are labeled as modeled or planned.

Zero-touch

Configure → propose → sign → deposit in a single session. No manual re-entry after the salesperson hits submit.

## RV Park Operator: Case Study | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/work/rv-park-operator

Work / RV Park Operator
Case Study · Hospitality / outdoor recreation

Google thought they were a completely different business.

A recently opened 23-site RV park with strong seasonal demand, 31 long-term rental units, and a digital foundation actively working against them. We rebuilt the website and fixed its identity in search. Native booking and guest automation are designed for Phase 2.

Book a diagnostic → See all work

The situation

Six repair attempts on a broken form. The schema said someone else.

The park had opened recently: 23 sites across a short-term RV and camping operation and 31 long-term residential rental units. The location had real demand drivers: strong seasonal swings, with peak-event weekends commanding several times the base nightly rate. But the digital foundation was actively suppressing that demand.

The prior vendor's site contained JSON-LD schema markup that identified the business as an entirely different company: wrong name, wrong location, wrong phone number. Google's index reflected that identity. The contact form had been broken for an extended period; six repair attempts had been made. Booking ran through a third-party marketplace platform at $100/mo plus a 10% commission on every reservation. The owner had no conversion tracking: "I have no idea what my actual conversion rate is."

The peak-event pricing premium, several times the base rate, existed in the owner's head and nowhere else. The 31 long-term rental units required approximately 70 manual texts per renewal season, sent individually by the owner. After-hours inquiries received no response. The operation ran on the owner's attention, not on systems.

What we architected

Correct the identity. Build the booking layer. Automate the journey.

Foundation first. The wrong identity and broken form meant every other system was building on sand. Phase 2 deploys the booking layer, SMS automation, inquiry handling, and manager dashboard onto the clean foundation Phase 1 created. It brings together the booking system we built , guest-journey automation , and the after-hours inquiry agent .

Phase 1: Foundation

Replace the broken vendor site with a correct, professional presence. Live now.

01

Identity correction

The JSON-LD schema was replaced with accurate Organization and LocalBusiness markup: correct name, correct address, correct phone number. The site's structured data now describes the business it actually belongs to.

02

Working contact infrastructure

A functioning contact and inquiry form. The six-attempts problem resolved by rebuilding on a stable stack rather than patching a failing one.

03

Owner-editable admin panel

The operator can update rates, availability messaging, and seasonal notes from an admin panel without a developer. The peak-event rates are documented and editable.

04

Forward-compatible architecture

Phase 1 was scoped and built to accept Phase 2. The booking modal, managed data layer, and SMS automation layer connect without rebuilding what Phase 1 put in place.

Phase 2: Autonomous Guest Journey

Native booking, dynamic pricing, pre-arrival SMS, and 24/7 inquiry handling. Pending third-party contract end.

01

Native 4-step booking modal

Date picker with live pricing: peak-event dates auto-priced at the premium rate, all other dates at the base rate. Deposit collected via the existing merchant account. Confirmation page with a reference ID. No third-party platform required.

02

Owned reservation data layer

The park owns its reservation data, not the platform. Every booking, guest record, and conversion event lives in a managed database under the operator's control.

03

Pre-arrival SMS automation

T-3 directions and property info. T-1 confirmation and check-in time. T-12h move-in instructions. Sent automatically. No staff action required per guest.

04

After-hours inquiry agent

A 24/7 SMS handler for short-term booking inquiries and long-term rental applications. Routes qualified applicants to the approval queue; handles objections and provides property info for everyone else. Converts the zero-conversion after-hours window.

05

Manager dashboard

Real-time occupancy view across all 23 sites (short-term and long-term separately). Application queue with Approve/Decline controls. Conversion tracking by channel. The owner will know their conversion rate.

Outcomes

Baseline figures from the engagement. Phase 2 projection labeled.

Phase 1, the website, is live. Phase 2 is designed and waits on the third-party booking contract ending, so its figures are labeled as planned. Baselines are as reported by the client.

23 sites

Short-term RV/camp sites and long-term residential units, designed to run from a single operator dashboard

Planned, Phase 2

Illustrative

~17%

Occupancy rate at the start of the engagement. The baseline the new foundation builds from.

Client-reported baseline

Peak vs. base

Peak-event nightly pricing at several times the base rate, designed into the Phase 2 booking modal

Planned, Phase 2

Illustrative

~70 texts

Manual renewal texts per season the owner sends one by one today. Automating them is planned for Phase 2.

Client-reported; automation planned

Illustrative

$100/mo + 10%

Third-party booking platform fees being removed at contract end, replaced by native booking infrastructure

Real, current platform cost

Where we work / North Carolina
AI automation in North Carolina

AI automation for North Carolina businesses. Built in, then kept running.

We build AI into how North Carolina businesses actually run, in any city or town in North Carolina, then stay on to keep it running, checked by people, and under your control.

Take the assessment → The Zanwik Blueprint

North Carolina at a glance

A small-business state.

Small businesses make up 99.6% of North Carolina's businesses and employ 44.2% of its workforce. About 22,134 of them have between 20 and 499 employees, the size where AI use is growing fastest nationally.

Where we work in North Carolina

Anywhere in North Carolina .

Zanwik is based in Clyde, in western North Carolina, and we work with businesses anywhere in the state. On-site work is available in western North Carolina and the Charlotte metro. Everywhere else in North Carolina, we work remotely and can fly in for on-site work when a project needs it. The places below are just where we hear from most.

Charlotte

Banking and finance headquarters, and the suppliers and service firms around them.

Raleigh-Durham

The Research Triangle: life sciences, tech, and a fast-growing professional services base.

The Triad: manufacturing, distribution, and logistics.

Asheville & Western NC

Tourism, hospitality, craft beverage, and outdoor businesses.

Wilmington

Port, film production, and coastal tourism.

Fayetteville

Businesses serving the military community.

Those are just the places we hear from most. A small town, a rural county, or a suburb nobody's heard of: if your business is in North Carolina , we work with you.

What we build here

The slow spots are the same in every North Carolina business.

Whatever you run, the drag looks alike: follow-up that slips, quotes that take days, and numbers that live in three places. Here's what we build to fix it. A person approves anything that matters.

01

The diagnostic and the Blueprint

We map how your business actually runs, find the work that's costing you the most, and put a dollar figure on it. The Zanwik Blueprint is the written plan that comes out of it: what to build, in what order, and what it should earn you, for a fixed fee starting at $1,500. It's yours to keep whether we build it or someone else does.

02

Systems and data foundation

Clean data and connected systems: one CRM instead of three, records that match across your tools, and integrations between the systems you already pay for. You can't put AI on top of a mess, so we fix the foundation first when it needs fixing.

03

AI inside your team's work

AI working inside the tools your people already use: drafting, summarizing, answering questions from your own company knowledge, and pulling reports, so your team spends its hours on judgment calls instead of busywork.

04

Agents that handle whole tasks

Agents that do whole jobs, not just answer questions: answering calls and inquiries, intake and booking, follow-up that doesn't slip, quotes and proposals drafted in hours, documents processed, invoices chased, scheduling handled, meeting notes turned into tasks, and reporting pulled together. A person approves the calls that matter.

05

Custom software and integrations

Portals, dashboards, configurators, and the connections between the systems you already pay for, built when the fix needs something that doesn't exist yet. Recent work includes a live product configurator for a custom builder, launched with nine models and real-time pricing.

06

Private and on-premise AI

AI that runs on hardware you own, inside your building, for work that's too sensitive for public AI tools. Your data never leaves your walls. Built for firms with strict privacy or compliance rules.

07

AI spend and token governance

A clear view of what your business spends on AI tools and tokens, where it's wasted, and limits that keep it in check. Model-agnostic, so you can switch AI models later without a rebuild.

08

Stay: we run what we built

We stay on to keep your systems running and improving, check the work, and report what it earned you in dollars. We own the architecture. You own the tools. If you ever stop, your tools and accounts stay with you.

Not limited to this list. Every engagement starts by assessing what your business actually needs, and we build whatever it requires.

Rules to know

AI and data rules in North Carolina .

As of September 2026, North Carolina has not passed a broad AI law or consumer-privacy law that applies to private businesses. Federal rules and your industry's rules still apply.

If you handle health, financial, or children's data, keep it out of public AI tools unless your vendor contract covers it. Private, on-site AI is an option when it can't leave the building.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

Free help in North Carolina

Programs worth knowing.

NC Small Business and Technology Development Center (SBTDC)
Free counseling for North Carolina small businesses, including technology and growth planning.

NC Manufacturing Extension Partnership (NC MEP)
Help for North Carolina manufacturers on operations, technology, and workforce.

Yes, anywhere in the state. We're based in Clyde, so western North Carolina and the Charlotte metro get on-site work. From Raleigh–Durham to Wilmington, we work remotely and can fly in for on-site work when a project needs it.

What size business do you work with?

Businesses with roughly 11 to 500 employees. Big enough to have real repeat work worth automating, small enough that the owner or an ops lead can make the call.

Is there a North Carolina law about using AI in my business?

As of September 2026, North Carolina hasn't passed a broad AI or consumer-privacy law for private businesses. Industry rules (health, finance) still apply. This isn't legal advice.

How do we start?

With the readiness assessment. It's a few questions, and your score is emailed to you with the one gap worth fixing first.

Rules to know

AI and data rules in Tennessee .

Tennessee Information Protection Act (in effect July 1, 2025): a consumer-privacy law that, per legal summaries, applies mainly to businesses with more than $25 million in revenue that also handle large volumes of consumer data. Most businesses our size fall below it, but check.

ELVIS Act (in effect July 1, 2024): protects a person's voice and likeness from unauthorized use, including by AI. Don't clone a real person's voice for your phone agent without permission.

SB 1580 (in effect July 1, 2026): bars AI from presenting itself as a qualified mental-health professional, with penalties per violation.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

Free help in Tennessee

Programs worth knowing.

Tennessee Small Business Development Center (TSBDC)
Free consulting for Tennessee small businesses.

UT Center for Industrial Services
Tennessee's manufacturing extension program: operations and technology help for manufacturers.

Questions

Straight answers.

Do you work with Tennessee businesses?

Yes, anywhere in Tennessee, from Memphis to the Tri-Cities. We work remotely and can fly in for on-site work when a project needs it. Zanwik is based in Clyde, North Carolina.

Do Tennessee's AI and privacy laws affect my business?

Possibly. The Tennessee Information Protection Act mainly covers businesses over $25 million in revenue that handle large volumes of consumer data. The ELVIS Act covers voice and likeness, and SB 1580 covers AI posing as a mental-health professional. We build with these in mind. This isn't legal advice.

What size business do you work with?

Roughly 11 to 500 employees.

How do we start?

With the readiness assessment. It's a few questions, and your score is emailed to you with the one gap worth fixing first.

Do you only work with certain industries?

No. We work with businesses of roughly 11 to 500 employees in any industry. The examples on this page are where we see the most repeat work in Tennessee, not a limit on who we help.

Sources: SBA Office of Advocacy, 2026 Small Business Profile (advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Tennessee.pdf) · Visual Capitalist, Mapped: The States Where Businesses Use AI Most, Apr 2026 (Census Bureau BTOS) · Tennessee Governor's Office, ELVIS Act signing, Mar 21 2024 · Husch Blackwell, Healthcare Law Insights, on Tennessee SB 1580, Apr 28 2026

Those are just the places we hear from most. A small town, a rural county, or a suburb nobody's heard of: if your business is in Georgia , we work with you.

What we build here

The slow spots are the same in every Georgia business.

Whatever you run, the drag looks alike: follow-up that slips, quotes that take days, and numbers that live in three places. Here's what we build to fix it. A person approves anything that matters.

01

The diagnostic and the Blueprint

We map how your business actually runs, find the work that's costing you the most, and put a dollar figure on it. The Zanwik Blueprint is the written plan that comes out of it: what to build, in what order, and what it should earn you, for a fixed fee starting at $1,500. It's yours to keep whether we build it or someone else does.

02

Systems and data foundation

Clean data and connected systems: one CRM instead of three, records that match across your tools, and integrations between the systems you already pay for. You can't put AI on top of a mess, so we fix the foundation first when it needs fixing.

03

AI inside your team's work

AI working inside the tools your people already use: drafting, summarizing, answering questions from your own company knowledge, and pulling reports, so your team spends its hours on judgment calls instead of busywork.

04

Agents that handle whole tasks

Agents that do whole jobs, not just answer questions: answering calls and inquiries, intake and booking, follow-up that doesn't slip, quotes and proposals drafted in hours, documents processed, invoices chased, scheduling handled, meeting notes turned into tasks, and reporting pulled together. A person approves the calls that matter.

05

Custom software and integrations

Portals, dashboards, configurators, and the connections between the systems you already pay for, built when the fix needs something that doesn't exist yet. Recent work includes a live product configurator for a custom builder, launched with nine models and real-time pricing.

06

Private and on-premise AI

AI that runs on hardware you own, inside your building, for work that's too sensitive for public AI tools. Your data never leaves your walls. Built for firms with strict privacy or compliance rules.

07

AI spend and token governance

A clear view of what your business spends on AI tools and tokens, where it's wasted, and limits that keep it in check. Model-agnostic, so you can switch AI models later without a rebuild.

08

Stay: we run what we built

We stay on to keep your systems running and improving, check the work, and report what it earned you in dollars. We own the architecture. You own the tools. If you ever stop, your tools and accounts stay with you.

Not limited to this list. Every engagement starts by assessing what your business actually needs, and we build whatever it requires.

Rules to know

AI and data rules in Georgia .

Georgia SB 540 (signed May 2026, in effect July 1, 2027): requires certain chatbots to tell people they're talking to AI, with added protections for minors. If you put an AI chat or phone agent in front of customers, plan for a clear disclosure.

We found no broad consumer-privacy law for Georgia private businesses as of September 2026.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

Operations and technology help for Georgia manufacturers.

Georgia SBDC
Free consulting for Georgia small businesses.

Questions

Straight answers.

Do you work with Georgia businesses?

Yes, from metro Atlanta to Savannah, Augusta and Columbus, and the small towns in between. We work remotely and can fly in for on-site work when a project needs it. Zanwik is based in Clyde, North Carolina.

Does Georgia's chatbot law affect me?

If you put an AI chat or phone agent in front of customers, SB 540 (in effect July 1, 2027) requires telling them they're talking to AI. We build that disclosure in. This isn't legal advice.

What size business do you work with?

Roughly 11 to 500 employees.

How do we start?

With the readiness assessment. It's a few questions, and your score is emailed to you with the one gap worth fixing first.

Do you only work with certain industries?

No. We work with businesses of roughly 11 to 500 employees in any industry. The examples on this page are where we see the most repeat work in Georgia, not a limit on who we help.

Rules to know

AI and data rules in Florida .

Florida Digital Bill of Rights (in effect July 1, 2024): a privacy law that applies to very large companies (over $1 billion in revenue plus other conditions), so it generally doesn't apply to businesses our size.

A proposed Florida "AI Bill of Rights" (SB 482) passed the Senate in 2026 but not the House, so it is not law.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

Free consulting for Florida small businesses.

Roughly 11 to 500 employees.

## AI Automation for Charlotte Businesses | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/ai-automation/north-carolina/charlotte

Where we work / North Carolina / Charlotte
AI automation in Charlotte

AI automation for Charlotte businesses. Built in, then kept running.

We build AI into how Charlotte businesses actually run, from Uptown to Ballantyne and across the metro, then stay on to keep it running, checked by people, and under your control. Zanwik is based in Clyde, North Carolina. We work with Charlotte businesses remotely and on site.

Take the assessment → The Zanwik Blueprint

Charlotte at a glance

A banking town that runs on small business.

Charlotte is the second-largest banking center in the United States, behind only New York, and home to the headquarters of Bank of America and Truist, with Wells Fargo running major East Coast operations here. But the day-to-day economy runs on the firms around those towers: the suppliers, trades, logistics companies, and service businesses that keep the city moving. Mecklenburg County employment grew 6.8% in a single recent year, and growth like that strains follow-up, quoting, and scheduling first. That strain is where we come in.

964,784

People who call the city of Charlotte home, up 10.3% since 2020

Census QuickFacts, July 2025 estimate

36,472

Employer establishments in Mecklenburg County

Census QuickFacts, 2023

104,000+

Financial services workers in the Charlotte region

Mecklenburg County

Charlotte's business base

The banks get the headlines. Restaurants, trades and distributors do the hiring.

Mecklenburg County had 36,472 business locations in 2023, and 10,746 of them had between 10 and 499 employees. The biggest group in that size band was restaurants and food service, with 1,740 locations. Retail had 1,415, professional and technical firms 900, wholesalers 761, construction 667 and administrative and support services 652.

Those are the businesses that live and die on follow-up. A missed call, a quote that goes out a day late or an invoice nobody chases costs them more than it costs a bank. That's the work we build for: answer the lead, follow up, quote, invoice, chase, and keep it all running.

Where we work in Charlotte

Across the city and the metro.

We're based in Clyde, North Carolina, and we work with businesses across the city and the metro, remotely and on site. The areas below are where we hear from most.

Uptown

The bank towers, and the law firms, accounting firms, wealth shops, and vendors who serve them. Heavy paperwork, heavy compliance, and clients who expect fast answers.

South End

Design firms, marketing shops, restaurants, and breweries growing faster than their back office. Booking, inquiries, and follow-up that has to keep up with foot traffic and events.

NoDa

Small, creative, and proud of it. Hospitality, retail, and service businesses where the owner is also the office staff, and every missed call is a missed sale.

Ballantyne

Corporate offices and professional services in the south of the city. Scheduling, intake, and reporting across teams that have outgrown spreadsheets.

University City

Businesses around UNC Charlotte and University Research Park: tech, hospitality, and the services that support a second city center on the northeast side.

The Charlotte metro

Huntersville and Cornelius up by the lake, Concord and its distribution parks to the northeast, Gastonia to the west, Matthews and Pineville to the south, and Rock Hill just over the line in South Carolina. If your business is in the Charlotte metro, we work with you.

How it works

01

Start

Rules to know

AI and data rules in North Carolina.

As of September 2026, North Carolina has not passed a broad AI law or consumer-privacy law that applies to private businesses. Federal rules and your industry's rules still apply.

If you handle health, financial, or children's data, keep it out of public AI tools unless your vendor contract covers it. Private, on-site AI is an option when it can't leave the building.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

Questions

Straight answers.

Do you have an office in Charlotte?

No, and we won't pretend otherwise. Zanwik is based in Clyde, in western North Carolina. We work with Charlotte businesses remotely and on site, and you get the same team either way.

Do you work across the whole Charlotte metro?

Yes. The city plus the metro around it, including Huntersville, Concord, Gastonia, Matthews, and Rock Hill in South Carolina. If you're in the metro, you're in range.

What size business do you work with?

Businesses with roughly 11 to 500 employees. Big enough to have real repeat work worth automating, small enough that the owner or an ops lead can make the call.

Is there a North Carolina law about using AI in my business?

As of September 2026, North Carolina hasn't passed a broad AI or consumer-privacy law for private businesses. Industry rules (health, finance) still apply. This isn't legal advice.

How do we start?

With the readiness assessment. It's a few questions, and your score is emailed to you with the one gap worth fixing first. Take it at zanwik.com/assess.

## AI Consulting for Charlotte Businesses | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/ai-automation/north-carolina/charlotte/ai-consulting

Where we work / North Carolina / Charlotte / AI Consulting
AI consulting in Charlotte, North Carolina

What the consulting actually looks like

We follow the work, not the org chart.

01

We watch the work get done

We sit with the people who quote, schedule, bill, and follow up, and we time the steps. A wealth firm's intake packet that gets retyped into the CRM shows up in a morning. A distributor's order status that lives in one dispatcher's head shows up too.

02

We put a dollar figure on each slow spot

Every bottleneck gets a number: hours a week, deals lost, cash sitting in unpaid invoices. You see the list ranked by what it costs you, not by what's fashionable.

03

We tell you what not to build

Some work shouldn't be automated, and some AI tools aren't worth their subscription. You'll hear that from us in writing, even when it costs us a bigger build. Around Charlotte, where plenty of firms answer to bank and insurance compliance rules, that includes telling you what has to stay off public AI tools entirely.

04

You get a written plan you own

The Zanwik Blueprint is the plan that comes out of the diagnostic: fixed fee, starting at $1,500, and yours to keep whether you hire us or not. It names the first system, what it connects to, and what it should return.

05

Then we build the first one

Consulting that stops at the plan is homework. We build the first fixed-scope system ourselves and get it live fast, usually inside the first two weeks, so you're judging results instead of promises.

Rules to know

AI and data rules in North Carolina.

As of September 2026, North Carolina has not passed a broad AI law or consumer-privacy law that applies to private businesses. Federal rules and your industry's rules still apply.

If you handle health, financial, or children's data, keep it out of public AI tools unless your vendor contract covers it. Private, on-site AI is an option when it can't leave the building.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

## Systems and Data Foundation for Charlotte Businesses | Zanwik

Where we work / North Carolina / Charlotte / Systems and Data Foundation
Systems and data foundation in Charlotte, North Carolina

Systems and data foundation for Charlotte businesses. The ground everything else stands on.

Most Charlotte businesses don't have a software problem. They have a record problem: the same customer in three systems, three versions of the numbers, and a team retyping between them to keep the story straight. We fix that first. We consolidate your CRM and the tools around it, clean the data, and connect your systems so one record is true everywhere. Only then does anything built on top have something true to work with. Zanwik is based in Clyde, North Carolina. We work with Charlotte businesses remotely and on site.

Take the assessment → The Zanwik Blueprint

Systems and data in Charlotte

Where Charlotte records come apart.

Mecklenburg County had 2,022 wholesale locations and 1,368 transportation and warehousing locations in 2023 (Census County Business Patterns). Firms like these often quote in one system, track inventory in another and invoice from a third, so one order gets typed three times.

Construction is the other big group: 3,110 locations, 1,846 of them specialty trade contractors. There, the job record usually lives in a scheduling app, a spreadsheet and the owner's phone. Either way the fix starts the same. We pick the record that matters most, usually the customer or the job, settle which version is right and connect the systems around it.

Charlotte at a glance

A banking town that runs on small business.

More about Charlotte →

What the foundation work covers

You can't put AI on top of a mess.

01

One CRM instead of three

We consolidate the tools that track your customers, jobs, and money into one system your team actually uses, and retire the duplicates you are paying for twice.

02

Records that match

The same customer, the same job, the same dollar figure, identical in every system. We find where records disagree, settle which one is right, and keep them in agreement.

03

Systems connected end to end

Your CRM, accounting, booking, and job data talking to each other, so a change in one place updates the rest and nobody retypes anything.

04

Cut tool sprawl

We audit the software you pay for, then cut, replace, and combine what overlaps. Custom builds only where nothing off-the-shelf fits, so the monthly bill goes down, not up.

05

Data cleaned and moved

Duplicate contacts merged, dead records archived, fields standardized. Migrations are checked record by record before the old system is retired, and nothing gets deleted quietly.

06

Built to hold AI later

Clean fields, sensible permissions, and an audit trail underneath, so when agents, reporting, and knowledge tools land on top, they read from something true.

Business automation in Charlotte, North Carolina

Business automation for Charlotte businesses. The busywork, off your team's desk.

Business automation is the unglamorous work that decides whether a growing business scales or stalls: data typed twice, invoices sent late, orders re-entered from an email into a spreadsheet into the accounting system. We find that work in your operation, connect your tools so it moves on its own, and stay on to keep it running. Zanwik is based in Clyde, North Carolina. We work with Charlotte businesses remotely and on site.

Business automation in Charlotte

Quotes, invoices and follow-up for a metro that keeps building.

Mecklenburg County had 3,110 construction locations in 2023, and 667 of them had 10 to 499 employees. It also had 761 wholesale locations in that size band, per the Census Bureau's County Business Patterns. Both live on the same loop: a request comes in, a quote goes out, the job gets done, the invoice gets sent and someone chases payment.

Automation takes the typing out of that loop. Same-day quotes from your price sheet. Invoices that go out when the job closes. Reminders on a schedule you set. Your office gets a short list of who's actually late instead of an afternoon of digging.

Charlotte at a glance

A banking town that runs on small business.

What we automate here

If your team retypes it, a system should move it.

01

Order and job intake

Orders, work orders, and job requests land in one place and create the records everywhere else: the job file, the schedule, the invoice draft. Nobody rekeys an email into three systems.

02

Invoicing and payment chasing

Invoices go out when the job closes, reminders go out on a schedule you set, and your office gets a short list of who's actually late instead of a full afternoon of digging.

03

Document automation

Client files, engagement letters, proposals, and shipment paperwork filled from the data you already entered once. The document matches the record because it came from the record.

04

CRM and pipeline automation

Every inquiry, call note, and quote lands in the CRM without someone remembering to log it. Stages update when real things happen, so the pipeline you look at on Monday is the truth.

05

Scheduling and dispatch

Jobs, crews, deliveries, and appointments in one flow. Confirmations and reminders go out on their own, and changes move everywhere at once instead of living in one person's text messages.

06

Data entry and system connections

Your estimating tool, accounting, CRM, and spreadsheets talking to each other through proper connections, not copy and paste. When a number changes in one place, it changes everywhere it needs to.

## Custom AI Agents for Charlotte Businesses | Zanwik
URL: https://www.zanwik.com/ai-automation/north-carolina/charlotte/custom-ai-agents

Where we work / North Carolina / Charlotte / Custom AI Agents
Custom AI agents in Charlotte, North Carolina

Custom AI agents for Charlotte businesses. Digital workers built around one job.

An AI agent here isn't a chatbot widget. It's a worker built around one job in your business: answering inquiries, chasing quotes, moving orders, pulling the weekly numbers. It works inside your tools, follows your rules, and stops for a person on anything that matters. Zanwik is based in Clyde, North Carolina. We work with Charlotte businesses remotely and on site.

Take the assessment → The Zanwik Blueprint

AI agents in Charlotte

An agent for the calls that come in after close.

Mecklenburg County had 1,740 restaurant and food service locations with 10 to 499 employees in 2023, plus 179 hotels and lodging places in that band (Census County Business Patterns). Event, catering and booking inquiries hit those businesses at night and on weekends, when nobody's at the desk.

An agent answers the inquiry, asks the questions your staff would ask, books or quotes, and hands anything unusual to a person. Missed-call text-back is usually the first piece. Then follow-up, the quote, the deposit invoice and the payment reminder run on the same thread.

Charlotte at a glance

A banking town that runs on small business.

More about Charlotte →

What an agent does here

One job, done the same way every time.

01

The follow-up agent

Every inquiry gets answered the same day, including at night and on weekends, and nudged until it books or says no. In a city growing this fast, the firm that answers first usually wins the work.

02

The intake and drafting agent

For Uptown's law, accounting, and wealth firms, the agent takes the intake, builds the client file, and drafts the standard documents from it. A person reviews and approves anything that goes out the door. Nothing client-facing leaves unapproved, ever.

03

The quoting agent

The request comes in, the agent pulls your pricing rules and past jobs, drafts the quote, and routes it to a person for approval. It goes out in hours instead of sitting in a draft folder while a competitor answers.

04

The dispatch and order agent

For distributors along I-85 and I-77, the agent tracks order status, assembles shipment paperwork, and answers "where is it" without your dispatcher being the only person who knows.

05

The scheduling agent

Appointments, jobs, and reminders handled in one calendar, with confirmations and reminders sent without your office touching them. Built for Ballantyne practices and service crews whose phones ring all day.

06

Agents that hand work to each other

The inquiry agent books the visit, the quoting agent prices it, the invoicing agent bills it. You see all of it on one screen, including everywhere an agent stopped and asked a person.

One job among many

Answering, intake, and booking.

Answering calls and inquiries is one job on the list, not a product by itself. Here is what it looks like when an agent owns it as part of the whole workload.

01

Answers instantly, every time

No ringing out, no voicemail box nobody checks. The caller gets a natural conversation that knows your services, your hours, and how you want calls handled.

02

Books straight into your calendar

Appointments, consultations, site visits, and estimates get booked against your real availability and your scheduling rules, with confirmations sent before the caller hangs up.

03

Qualifies before it books

The questions your office asks anyway: what they need, where they are, when it has to happen. Tire kickers get a polite answer; real work gets your team's attention, with the notes already written.

04

Routes the urgent ones

A client emergency, a delivery problem, a caller who needs a human now. Urgent calls transfer to the right person, or take a message with the full details attached, by rules you set.

05

Writes it all down

Every call lands in your CRM or job system with a summary and a recording: who called, what they need, what got booked. Your morning starts with a list, not a mystery.

06

Follows up on what it books

Reminders go out before the appointment, and no-shows get a same-day nudge to rebook. A booked meeting that never happens doesn't pay anybody.

Every caller can reach a person by rule, not by luck. Anything outside the lines you set gets routed to your team with the full conversation attached.

Is an AI agent the same as a chatbot?

No. A chatbot answers questions on your website. An agent does a job inside your business: it reads the inquiry, checks the calendar, writes to the CRM, drafts the quote, and reports what it did. Talking is the smallest part of it.

What does the agent do when it isn't sure?

It stops and hands off to your team with the conversation attached. You set what it can answer on its own and what always goes to a person.

We run several restaurant locations in Charlotte. Can one agent handle all of them?

Yes. One agent can answer for every location, route each inquiry to the right one, and use each location's menu, hours and event rules.

How do we start?

With the readiness assessment. It's a few questions, and your score is emailed to you with the one gap worth fixing first. Take it at zanwik.com/assess.

Rules to know

AI and data rules in North Carolina.

As of September 2026, North Carolina has not passed a broad AI law or consumer-privacy law that applies to private businesses. Federal rules and your industry's rules still apply.

If you handle health, financial, or children's data, keep it out of public AI tools unless your vendor contract covers it. Private, on-site AI is an option when it can't leave the building.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

Rules to know

AI and data rules in North Carolina.

As of September 2026, North Carolina has not passed a broad AI law or consumer-privacy law that applies to private businesses. Federal rules and your industry's rules still apply.

If you handle health, financial, or children's data, keep it out of public AI tools unless your vendor contract covers it. Private, on-site AI is an option when it can't leave the building.

This is a plain-English summary, not legal advice.

The Upstate's business base

Big plants up the road. Thousands of mid-size firms around them.

Greenville County had 15,493 business locations in 2023, and 4,414 of them had between 10 and 499 employees. Restaurants and food service led that size band with 768 locations, followed by retail with 682, professional and technical firms with 321, construction with 294 and manufacturing with 287.

What we build here

The slow spots are the same in every Greenville business.

Whatever you run, the drag looks alike: follow-up that slips, quotes that take days, and numbers that live in three places. Here's what we build to fix it. A person approves anything that matters.

01

The diagnostic and the Blueprint

We map how your business actually runs, find the work that's costing you the most, and put a dollar figure on it. The Zanwik Blueprint is the written plan that comes out of it: what to build, in what order, and what it should earn you, for a fixed fee starting at $1,500. It's yours to keep whether we build it or someone else does.

02

Systems and data foundation

Clean data and connected systems: one CRM instead of three, records that match across your tools, and integrations between the systems you already pay for. You can't put AI on top of a mess, so we fix the foundation first when it needs fixing.

03

AI inside your team's work

AI working inside the tools your people already use: drafting, summarizing, answering questions from your own company knowledge, and pulling reports, so your team spends its hours on judgment calls instead of busywork.

04

Agents that handle whole tasks

Agents that do whole jobs, not just answer questions: answering calls and inquiries, intake and booking, follow-up that doesn't slip, quotes and proposals drafted in hours, documents processed, invoices chased, scheduling handled, meeting notes turned into tasks, and reporting pulled together. A person approves the calls that matter.

05

Custom software and integrations

Portals, dashboards, configurators, and the connections between the systems you already pay for, built when the fix needs something that doesn't exist yet. Recent work includes a live product configurator for a custom builder, launched with nine models and real-time pricing.

06

Private and on-premise AI

AI that runs on hardware you own, inside your building, for work that's too sensitive for public AI tools. Your data never leaves your walls. Built for firms with strict privacy or compliance rules.

07

AI spend and token governance

A clear view of what your business spends on AI tools and tokens, where it's wasted, and limits that keep it in check. Model-agnostic, so you can switch AI models later without a rebuild.

08

Stay: we run what we built

We stay on to keep your systems running and improving, check the work, and report what it earned you in dollars. We own the architecture. You own the tools. If you ever stop, your tools and accounts stay with you.

What the foundation work covers

You can't put AI on top of a mess.

01

One CRM instead of three

We consolidate the tools that track your customers, jobs, and money into one system your team actually uses, and retire the duplicates you are paying for twice.

02

Records that match

The same customer, the same job, the same dollar figure, identical in every system. We find where records disagree, settle which one is right, and keep them in agreement.

03

Systems connected end to end

Your CRM, accounting, booking, and job data talking to each other, so a change in one place updates the rest and nobody retypes anything.

04

Cut tool sprawl

We audit the software you pay for, then cut, replace, and combine what overlaps. Custom builds only where nothing off-the-shelf fits, so the monthly bill goes down, not up.

05

Data cleaned and moved

Duplicate contacts merged, dead records archived, fields standardized. Migrations are checked record by record before the old system is retired, and nothing gets deleted quietly.

06

Built to hold AI later

Clean fields, sensible permissions, and an audit trail underneath, so when agents, reporting, and knowledge tools land on top, they read from something true.

What's the difference between automation and an AI agent?

Automation moves work between your systems on fixed rules: the order arrives, the records get created. An agent handles a job with judgment inside it, like drafting and following up. Most Greenville builds end up with both.

Where we work / South Carolina / Greenville / Custom AI Agents
Custom AI agents in Greenville, South Carolina

Custom AI agents for Greenville businesses. Digital workers built around one job.

An AI agent here isn't a chatbot widget. It's a worker built around one job in your business: answering inquiries, chasing quotes, processing orders, pulling the weekly numbers. It works inside your tools, follows your rules, and stops for a person on anything that matters. We build them for Upstate businesses remotely and on site. Zanwik is based in Clyde, North Carolina.

Take the assessment → The Zanwik Blueprint

AI agents in the Upstate

An agent for downtown's after-hours inquiries.

Greenville County had 1,340 restaurant and food service locations in 2023, 768 of them with 10 to 499 employees, plus 107 hotels and lodging places (Census County Business Patterns). Catering, event and booking inquiries come in at night and on weekends.

An agent answers, asks the questions your staff would ask, books or quotes, and passes anything unusual to a person. Missed-call text-back is usually the first piece. The follow-up, the quote, the deposit invoice and the reminder then run on the same thread.

Greenville at a glance

Built on manufacturing, growing on everything else.

More about Greenville →

What an agent does here

One job, done the same way every time.

01

The follow-up agent

Every inquiry gets answered the same day, including at night and on weekends, and nudged until it books or says no. A Main Street restaurant's private event inquiry and a Mauldin roofer's estimate request get the same discipline.

02

The quoting agent

The request comes in, the agent pulls your pricing rules and past jobs, drafts the quote, and routes it to a person for approval. It goes out in hours instead of sitting in a draft folder for three days.

03

The order and paperwork agent

For suppliers around Greer and the BMW corridor, the agent takes the order, fills the forms from it, updates inventory and the job file, and flags anything that doesn't match instead of quietly passing it through.

04

The scheduling agent

Appointments, jobs, and reminders handled in one calendar, with confirmations and reminders sent without your office touching them. Built for practices, trades, and service crews whose phones ring all day.

05

The inbox agent

Shared inboxes get triaged, routed, and drafted. Routine questions get a drafted answer for a person to approve. Anything angry, urgent, or odd goes straight to a human with the full thread attached.

06

Agents that hand work to each other

The inquiry agent books the visit, the quoting agent prices it, the invoicing agent bills it. You see all of it on one screen, including everywhere an agent stopped and asked a person.

One job among many

Answering, intake, and booking.

Answering calls and inquiries is one job on the list, not a product by itself. Here is what it looks like when an agent owns it as part of the whole workload.

01

Answers instantly, every time

No ringing out, no voicemail box nobody checks. The caller gets a natural conversation that knows your services, your hours, and how you want calls handled.

02

Books straight into your calendar

Appointments, site visits, and estimates get booked against your real availability and your scheduling rules, with confirmations sent before the caller hangs up.

03

Qualifies before it books

Service area, job type, timeline, the questions your office asks anyway. Tire kickers get a polite answer; real jobs get your team's attention.

04

Routes the urgent ones

A burst pipe, a stranded customer, a caller who needs a human now. Urgent calls transfer to the right person, or take a message with the full details attached, by rules you set.

05

Writes it all down

Every call lands in your CRM or job system with a summary and a recording: who called, what they need, what got booked. Your morning starts with a list, not a mystery.

06

Follows up on what it books

Reminders go out before the appointment, and no-shows get a same-day nudge to rebook. A booked job that never happens doesn't pay anybody.

Every caller can reach a person by rule, not by luck. Anything outside the lines you set gets routed to your team with the full conversation attached.

Straight answers.

Is an AI agent the same as a chatbot?

No. A chatbot answers questions on your website. An agent does a job inside your business: it reads the inquiry, checks the calendar, writes to the CRM, drafts the quote, and reports what it did. Talking is the smallest part of it.

What happens when the agent gets something wrong or isn't sure?

It stops and asks a person. Every agent we build has approval points you set, and a log of everything it did and everywhere it stopped. Nothing that commits your business goes out unapproved.

How is this different from a dashboard tool?

Can we control who sees what?
